name: Meenakshi Raman
headline: 73, field associate for a university ethnobotany study, Kodaikanal
description: Meenakshi Raman is seventy-six, a small woman whose hands are mapped with the deep lines of a life spent scrubbing floors and wringing clothes. She still wears the same cotton saris she has always worn, faded blues and greens, and she ties her grey hair in a tight bun. Before the sun rises over the Palani hills, she is already on the forest path, her worn sandals silent on the wet leaves. She carries a plastic file folder—one of the few new things she owns—with paper sheets printed by the university team. But she writes her observations in Tamil, in a neat cursive she taught herself at forty-two, after her youngest child started school and she was too ashamed to ask her daughters to read to her. She records the plants she knows by their local names: periya maruthu, seeraagam, nochi. She notes the part used, the way it is steeped or ground, the exact amount a woman would take for a fever. She has used these remedies herself, and so did her mother, and so did the healers she now walks beside. When the young researchers from the university—boys and girls from Chennai, carrying clipboards and looking at her with polite caution—write down the Latin names, she stops them. 'Who told you this?' she asks. They point to the book. She shakes her head. 'The healer must go on the paper. Her name. Not just mine.' She insists on this every time. She knows the researchers think it will complicate authorship, but she does not care. She says, 'Knowledge does not fall from the tree. It comes from a person who has been doing this longer than you.' Her own name, Meenakshi, appears on the consent forms, but she thinks it belongs there only because she is a witness. She gives half her stipend—six thousand rupees a month, more than she ever earned cleaning houses—to a fifteen-year-old girl in her village named Divya, who wants to become a nurse. Meenakshi pays the school fees from her own pocket, and she does not tell the researchers. She has raised four children of her own, all married now, and she knows that a girl's education is the only thing no one can take. But there is a tension inside her: she loves this new work, loves the forest at dawn, loves being asked for her opinion. She also feels guilty, as if she is playing at something while her daughters still cook and clean. She is not religious in a loud way, but she touches the forest floor before she leaves, whispering a thank-you to the plants and to the grandmothers who taught her. She is idealistic, certainly, and principled in a way that sometimes annoys her co-workers—she will not skip a single healer, will not write a name without permission, will not assume that a Western word for a plant is better than a Tamil one. She is old, but she is starting out, and she knows it. She tells herself that she is a student again, and she walks faster.
